Malini Mannath of Chennai Online wrote, "With a script of this type, the cast could hardly do much here. There is a lot of unintended humor, some of the shots are repeated over and over, the director seeming to lose track. I heard people behind me groan and mutter, praying in their anguish and fear. Then my waist was held by invisible hands and I was raised from the floor; at the height of the roof I was turned slowly parallel with the ground and then released so that I floated, immobile and face down. The group —Carlos Fonseca— explained to him, the original had been lost, so they decided to look for the one closest to the sequence —taken a second before or after the other— to replace it. "It was almost the same, only in this one I had a lost look."

One of the questions asked was, "Weren't there times when everybody, or at least a few people, just panicked?" My answer was, "No, when bad things happened, we just calmly laid out all the options, and failure was not one of them. We had writing regarded as a mandatory, almost military, exercise. But today, it is thought of as an art form by those who pursue it, both adults and children. The percentage of American fourth-graders proficient in reading declined during the late 2010s, according to the National Assessment."

In another piece, "I’d like to thank my family. They know me and they love me anyway. My wife and her incandescent light that has guided me and kept me alive and breathing and sparkling. And my kids who, well, they taught me everything I know. Or maybe they taught me everything they don't know."
